meta.title: CrashFree India — State Road-Safety Governance Dataset
meta.description: Consolidated dataset merging 12 state-level road-safety governance and key-individual research files, each independently self-audited (fresh-search re-derivation + active disconfirming-evidence search) per research-rules.md. Every source citation from the original files is preserved. Every fact still flagged as UNVERIFIED / LIKELY STALE / PARTIALLY VERIFIED after the audit is carried forward here as a structured 'flag' object (badge) rather than prose, for direct rendering in a dashboard UI.

flag_resolution_category_key.a: A genuine, documented second/third attempt was made (≥2 search angles) but could not surface 2 independent corroborating sources.
flag_resolution_category_key.b: The ambiguity is genuinely unresolved in present-day reality (e.g. a contested jurisdiction, an active court stay, a transfer too recent to be reflected in any published source).

state_files.rajasthan: (added as 13th pilot state, 25 Sept 2026 — no original .md file; researched directly into this schema)

notable_corrections.summary: Deputy CM Ajit Pawar had died (28 Jan 2026) and was still listed as a serving minister — the single most significant correction across all 12 files.
The file's claim that no PWD Minister of State existed was a factual error — Brijesh Singh has held the post continuously since 2022.
The Road Construction Minister's name ("Kumar Dhirendra") did not match any source and was corrected to Kumar Shailendra; the Patna DM (who chairs the city's Road Safety Committee) had been replaced.
An active ED money-laundering investigation into the sitting PWD Minister, breaking two days before this audit, was entirely new information with direct bearing on CrashFree India's engagement plan.
Active, unresolved High Court litigation over the removal of the HYDRAA Commissioner was likewise new and directly relevant.
Resolved a standing priority question (whether the 2017 Road Safety Authority Bill was enacted) that determines which governance-model category the state belongs to.

tamil_nadu.political_context: Tamil Nadu held Legislative Assembly elections in 2026, with polling on 23 April 2026 and results on 4 May 2026. In a historic upset, the newly formed Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam (TVK), led by actor C. Joseph Vijay ("Vijay"), emerged as the single largest party with 108 of 234 seats — short of a majority, producing Tamil Nadu's first hung assembly. TVK formed a coalition government with Congress and other partners' support, and Vijay was sworn in as Chief Minister on 10 May 2026, ending the DMK's M. K. Stalin government; Stalin himself lost his own seat, the first incumbent CM to lose a TN election since Jayalalithaa in 1996. Any reference to a DMK-era minister or to "Chief Minister Stalin" is now historical only. CM Vijay personally retains Home/Police, General Administration, Municipal Administration, Urban and Water Supply, and several welfare portfolios — a structural pattern similar to Bihar/Jharkhand CMs who personally hold road-safety-adjacent departments. The cabinet sworn in on 10 May 2026 assigned Public Works (Buildings, Highways and Minor Ports) and Sports Development to Aadhav Arjuna; Transport to Vijay Tamilan Parthiban (who formally assumed the portfolio on 21 May 2026, per his own biography, distinct from the 10 May general oath date); Revenue and Disaster Management to K. A. Sengottaiyan; Rural Development and Water Resources to N. Anand; Health, Medical Education and Family Welfare to Dr. K. G. Arunraj; and Housing and Urban Development to B. Rajkumar. Dr. M. Sai Kumar, IAS continues as Chief Secretary, having been granted a further six-month service extension (1 September 2026 – 28 February 2027) under Rule 16(1) of the AIS (DCRB) Rules, 1958, ahead of his original 31 August 2026 retirement date; Dr. P. Senthilkumar serves as Additional Chief Secretary/Secretary-I to the CM and G. Laxmi Priya as Secretary-II to the CM (this last detail sourced only to Elets eGov and not independently re-corroborated in this pass). (Election/succession sources: Wikipedia — 2026 Tamil Nadu Legislative Assembly election, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_Tamil_Nadu_Legislative_Assembly_election; Wikipedia — M. K. Stalin, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M._K._Stalin.)

governance_bodies.name: Tamil Nadu Road Safety Policy (2007) and State Road Safety Machinery
governance_bodies.mandate: Tamil Nadu's Road Safety Policy dates to April 2007, making it, per its own framing, the first state-level road safety policy in India, predating the National Road Safety Policy (2010). Thrust areas: Engineering, Enforcement, and Education, plus data collection, safe infrastructure, driver safety, and Emergency Medical Response. The policy itself is not a legislative Act — no specific statutory reference was found, consistent with the MV Act Section 215 executive-rules model seen in Bihar/Jharkhand rather than Karnataka's dedicated 2017 Act.
governance_bodies.roads_owned: Not applicable — a policy framework, not a road-owning body.
governance_bodies.hierarchy: The 2007 policy proposed establishing a "lead agency" (a Road Safety Authority), but CAG's own analysis found the policy document does not detail that body's composition, chair, or meeting frequency, nor does it specify a dedicated road-safety budget/fund — a documented, independently-flagged gap in Tamil Nadu's own road-safety governance design.
governance_bodies.subordinate_bodies: District Road Safety Committees (DRSCs) — confirmed to exist at district level (e.g., Tirupathur district's own government portal lists a DRSC page), consistent with the national MV Act s.215(3) template, but composition, chair, and meeting frequency could not be independently fetched/confirmed in this pass (the district page itself returned a fetch error) — flagged as a priority gap.
governance_bodies.decision_making_power: Not established from the sources reviewed (Road Safety Authority/lead agency composition, chair, and meeting frequency not detailed in the policy itself).
governance_bodies.data_role: Data collection is named as one of the policy's thrust areas, but no dedicated statewide data mechanism is detailed in sources reviewed.
governance_bodies.performance_issues: Citizen consumer and civic Action Group (CAG), a Chennai-based consumer/civic NGO (distinct from the Comptroller and Auditor General), has run District Road Safety Conferences in multiple districts (Salem, Madurai, Cuddalore) and an annual Road Safety Week press campaign, indicating an active civil-society engagement channel with DRSCs — but statewide DRSC composition and cadence remain unconfirmed.
governance_bodies.meeting_frequency: Not independently confirmed in this pass (Tirupathur DRSC page fetch blocked; no statewide DRSC roster located).

governance_bodies.decision_making_power: For CrashFree India, IIT Madras' Centre of Excellence for Road Safety / RBG Labs is Tamil Nadu's closest analogue to NIMHANS in Karnataka — a technically credible, already-active research and data partner with a working relationship to Greater Chennai Traffic Police specifically, making it a strong first technical-partnership target rather than a purely political one.
governance_bodies.data_role: RBG Labs built the crash-data dashboard underlying the national iRAD system. In January 2026, this dashboard was reported as adopted by Odisha (integrating police/officials and citizen accident-reporting portals), with plans for pan-India expansion.
governance_bodies.performance_issues: The organiser.org article's TN-government-partnership framing was not itself independently corroborated with a Tamil Nadu government source in this pass (the article's confirmed content concerned Odisha's adoption) — the existence of an IIT Madras–TN government collaboration is corroborated by two other sources (careers360, Deccan Herald), but the specific current scope of that partnership was not established.
governance_bodies.meeting_frequency: Runs recurring, dated public programmes: "Road Safety Month 2024," a "Principals' Conclave" under "Training Young Minds," a recurring "Zero Accident Day" campaign with Greater Chennai Traffic Police, and an ongoing SNS Foundation research partnership.

delhi.political_context: Delhi is not a full state but a Union Territory with a Legislative Assembly (National Capital Territory of Delhi), governed under Article 239AA of the Constitution and the Government of National Capital Territory of Delhi Act, 1991. Police, Public Order, and Land are constitutionally excluded from the Delhi government's legislative and executive domain and remain with the Union Government acting through the Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) -- Delhi Police does not report to the Delhi Chief Minister or any Delhi minister at all, and its Commissioner is appointed directly by MHA order (confirmed by the MHA appointment order for Anurag Kumar, IPS, effective 17 July 2026, which also directed his predecessor to report to the Lieutenant Governor pending reposting). A 2023 amendment to the GNCTD Act (upheld in substance after the Supreme Court's 2023 Delhi services judgment prompted it) further gave the Lieutenant Governor sole discretionary authority, taking precedence over the Council of Ministers, on Delhi-Centre relations and on civil-service transfers/postings recommended by the National Capital Civil Services Authority -- meaning the LG is not a ceremonial figure in Delhi's governance in the way a Governor typically is in a full state. The Municipal Corporation of Delhi (MCD) layers a second executive duality on top of this: an elected, politically accountable Mayor (currently BJP's Pravesh Wahi) sits alongside a centrally posted IAS Municipal Commissioner (currently Sanjeev Khirwar) who holds the actual day-to-day executive and licensing/demolition authority -- a split that became acutely visible in September 2026 when a fatal Satya Niketan building collapse (seven dead) triggered public resignation demands directed at the Commissioner specifically, not the Mayor. In 2025-2026 all four apex offices changed hands: the BJP's Rekha Gupta became Chief Minister on 20 February 2025, ending a decade of AAP government under Arvind Kejriwal/Atishi; Vinai Kumar Saxena, LG since 2022, was moved to become LG of Ladakh and former career diplomat (and former Ambassador to the United States) Taranjit Singh Sandhu was sworn in as the new LG of Delhi on 11 March 2026, still in office as of this research pass (25 September 2026); BJP's Pravesh Wahi was elected Mayor of the MCD on 29 April 2026 with 156 of 165 votes cast, succeeding Raja Iqbal Singh (BJP, Apr 2025-Apr 2026), who had succeeded Mahesh Kumar Khichi (AAP, Nov 2024-Apr 2025) -- the point at which mayoral control passed from AAP to BJP; and Anurag Kumar, IPS (1994-batch, AGMUT cadre, a career intelligence officer previously Special Director of the Intelligence Bureau) was appointed Commissioner of Delhi Police on 17 July 2026, replacing Satish Golcha. Below the Commissioner, Delhi Police's Traffic Management Division -- the unit CrashFree India would work with on enforcement -- changed hands again in a Commissioner-ordered reshuffle of 43 IPS/DANIPS officers on 19 August 2026 (timed ahead of the 18th BRICS Summit, 12-13 September 2026), which returned 1996-batch IPS officer Ajay Chaudhary to head Traffic. On the elected side, the Legislative Assembly itself is lopsided (48 BJP to 22 AAP in the 8th Delhi Assembly), with former Chief Minister Atishi serving as Leader of the Opposition since February 2025. Practically, any Delhi engagement strategy must run on at least three separate, only partly overlapping tracks -- the elected Delhi government (PWD, Transport, MCD-adjacent civic matters), the Union-controlled Delhi Police/MHA enforcement track, and the MCD's own elected-Mayor/centrally-posted-Commissioner split -- with the Lieutenant Governor sitting institutionally above all three on several matters. This is a structure materially different from every full state in this document set, and CrashFree India asks that bundle enforcement, infrastructure, and civic-body commitments into a single proposal risk addressing an office that cannot actually deliver all three.

governance_bodies.name: Delhi Police (incl. Delhi Traffic Police) — a Union subject, not a Delhi government department
governance_bodies.mandate: Law enforcement, public order, and traffic policing in Delhi, including via a dedicated Traffic Management Division/Traffic Police wing.
governance_bodies.roads_owned: Not a road-owning body; holds enforcement authority over traffic on all Delhi roads regardless of the owning body (PWD, MCD, NDMC, Cantonment, or NHAI).
governance_bodies.hierarchy: Reports to the Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA), Government of India — NOT to the Delhi Chief Minister, any Delhi government minister, or a Delhi "Home Department" (no such department has operational authority over Delhi Police). This follows from Article 239AA of the Constitution and the Government of National Capital Territory of Delhi Act, 1991, under which Police, Public Order, and Land are constitutionally excluded from the Delhi government's legislative and executive domain. The Supreme Court's May 2023 Constitution Bench ruling (in the NCTD-vs-Union "Services" case) confirmed the LG's own discretionary powers extend only to these three excluded subjects (plus matters the President specifically delegates); the Government of NCT of Delhi (Amendment) Act, 2023 subsequently created the National Capital Civil Services Authority (NCCSA) to route transfer/posting decisions for other services through the LG, layering a further Union check onto the bureaucracy even outside Police/Land/Public Order. The Home Ministry has previously and explicitly rejected proposals to place a Traffic wing under the Delhi government.
governance_bodies.subordinate_bodies: Traffic Management Division/Traffic Police wing under a Special Commissioner of Police (Traffic), with a Joint Commissioner of Police (Traffic) as operational head beneath that tier and DCP (Traffic) posts below; DANIPS/IPS officer cadre subject to periodic MHA-ordered reshuffles. The exact reporting relationship between the Special CP (Traffic) and Joint CP (Traffic) posts was not independently confirmed with an official org chart in this pass (traffic.delhipolice.gov.in's detailed structure page was not fetchable).

governance_bodies.name: Unified Traffic and Transportation Infrastructure (Planning & Engineering) Centre (UTTIPEC)
governance_bodies.mandate: A dedicated multi-agency transport-planning and road-safety coordination body for the whole of the NCT of Delhi, established by DDA via a Gazette of India notification (S.O. No. 1903(E), dated 31.07.2008; regulatory modifications notified 07.08.2009) "to enhance mobility, reduce congestion and to promote traffic safety by adopting standard transport planning practices." Its stated focus areas explicitly include road safety audits, traffic engineering practices, capacity building, enforcement measures, lane-capacity and work-zone management, utilities coordination, and inter-agency organisational coordination for improved traffic management — making it the closest thing Delhi has to a single cross-jurisdictional road-safety planning table spanning PWD, MCD, NDMC, DDA, Delhi Metro, and Delhi Police.

governance_bodies.hierarchy: Constituted as the planning wing of the Delhi Development Authority; the Lieutenant Governor of Delhi (as DDA's Chairman) chairs UTTIPEC. It reviews and approves Multi-Modal-Integration (MMI) plans around Metro stations, road projects proposed by Delhi government agencies such as PWD, and related transportation/infrastructure projects across Delhi.

governance_bodies.name: Office of the Lieutenant Governor (LG) of Delhi / Raj Niwas
governance_bodies.mandate: Constitutional office representing the Union Government in the NCT of Delhi under Article 239AA, created by the Constitution (Sixty-ninth Amendment) Act, 1991. The LG is required to act on the aid and advice of the Delhi Council of Ministers EXCEPT on matters (a) beyond the Delhi Legislative Assembly's competence — Public Order, Police and Land, which are excluded from the Assembly's law-making power entirely — and (b) other matters where the President has specifically delegated discretionary power to the LG (post-2023, this includes recommendations of the National Capital Civil Services Authority on transfers/postings/vigilance for Delhi's civil services).
governance_bodies.roads_owned: Not a road-owning body directly, but chairs both DDA and UTTIPEC (see those entries) — the institutions holding Union land-use authority over road-network layout and multi-agency transport-infrastructure approval for Delhi — giving the LG's office an outsized institutional role in Delhi road planning despite not being an elected part of the road-owning agencies themselves.
governance_bodies.hierarchy: Apex representative of the Union Government within Delhi's governance structure; sits institutionally above the elected CM/Council of Ministers on the three excluded subjects, chairs the DDA and (via DDA) UTTIPEC, and is the appointing/administrative-control authority (through the Ministry of Home Affairs) for Delhi Police, NDMC's Chairperson, and MCD's Commissioner, even though NDMC formally reports to MoHUA and MCD is a separately elected body.
governance_bodies.subordinate_bodies: Not applicable in the usual departmental sense; the LG's office coordinates across DDA, UTTIPEC, and (via MHA) Delhi Police, NDMC, and civil-service postings through the National Capital Civil Services Authority (NCCSA), created by the Government of NCT of Delhi (Amendment) Act, 2023.

governance_bodies.mandate: The Union ministry exercising direct executive control over Police, Public Order, and (via DANICS/AGMUT cadre administration and the LG) Land and Services in the NCT of Delhi — the three subjects Article 239AA excludes from the elected Delhi government's domain, plus, since the 2023 amendment, a wider role in transfers/postings for Delhi's civil services generally.
governance_bodies.roads_owned: Not a road-owning body; relevant to CrashFree India because it is the actual appointing/reporting authority for Delhi Police (including Traffic Police), and — through Union appointment of AGMUT-cadre IAS officers — for MCD's Commissioner and NDMC's Chairperson as well, even though those two bodies formally report to MoHUA rather than MHA on other matters.

governance_bodies.hierarchy: Political head held personally by CM Rekha Gupta; as of 1 January 2026, restructured from 11 to 13 revenue districts (dissolving Shahdara district and creating Old Delhi, Central North, and Outer North districts), each headed by a Deputy Commissioner who also serves as District Magistrate, with 39 sub-divisions (up from 33/22 depending on the source's baseline) each headed by a Sub-Divisional Magistrate (SDM). The reorganisation was explicitly designed to align revenue-district boundaries with MCD's 12 administrative zones, NDMC, and Delhi Cantonment — a direct, government-acknowledged response to exactly the kind of cross-jurisdiction confusion this dashboard flags for road-safety purposes.

key_individuals.value_to_crashfree: Because she personally holds Revenue (which oversees the 11 district DM/DC offices that likely chair District Road Safety Committees) alongside Finance, she is structurally positioned for cross-department sign-off, but does not control Delhi Police (an MHA subject) or, directly, PWD/Transport (held by other ministers).

Institutionally, as the first BJP CM of Delhi in nearly three decades and the office-holder who must coordinate with a structurally powerful, BJP-aligned LG on services/civil-service matters, her incentive is to demonstrate visible, deliverable governance wins across her ten-plus portfolios ahead of the next Assembly cycle, and to avoid friction with the LG given the 2023 amendment's tilt toward LG discretion on cross-cutting matters. (Inference: because PWD's road-repair drive and Transport's Road Safety Work Plan already sit with ministers she appointed and continues to publicly back via portfolio allocation, she is unlikely to be an obstacle to road-safety asks routed through them, but nothing in the record shows her personally prioritising road safety as an issue in its own right.)

key_individuals.priorities_and_interests: Verma's brief tenure so far shows a pattern consistent with a senior AGMUT-cadre generalist administrator: his profile on appointment named a broad slate of civic-delivery priorities (pollution/Yamuna, traffic congestion, waste management, public transport, water supply) without singling out road safety, and his one clearly dated 2026 intervention -- the LG's direct tasking of his office on PG-building structural audits after the Satya Niketan collapse -- shows him as the administrative executor of LG- and CM-level civic-safety directives rather than an independent policy originator in this space. madhya_pradesh.political_context: Dr. Mohan Yadav (BJP) has served as Chief Minister of Madhya Pradesh since 13 December 2023, with Rajendra Shukla and Jagdish Devda as Deputy Chief Ministers (Wikipedia — Mohan Yadav: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohan_Yadav). The cabinet was sworn in and portfolios allocated on 25/30 December 2023, and a fresh 11 September 2026 re-audit independently re-confirmed all six road-safety-relevant portfolios directly against each minister's own Wikipedia biography, finding them unchanged apart from one narrow, dated exception: on 16 July 2026 the Animal Husbandry and Dairy Development portfolio was withdrawn from Minister of State Lakhan Patel and placed directly under the Chief Minister in a late-night notification (Goemkarponn, 16 July 2026: https://goemkarponn.com/late-night-portfolio-change-sparks-buzz-over-cabinet-reshuffle-in-madhya-pradesh/); that reshuffle does not touch any of the six road-safety-relevant portfolios. Separately, a Dainik Jagran (Madhya Pradesh) report circulating in 2026 discusses speculation about a larger cabinet reshuffle — triggered by Urban Development Minister Kailash Vijayvargiya's political standing after the Dec 2025-Jan 2026 Bhagirathpura (Indore) contaminated-water tragedy — naming Vijayvargiya, Prahlad Singh Patel, Dilip Ahirwar, and Radha Singh as ministers who "could" see portfolios changed, while explicitly stating "no official confirmation has come from the CM's office" and floating a possible window no earlier than mid-2026 (Dainik Jagran English: https://english.dainikjagranmpcg.com/states/madhya-pradesh/seo-headline-mp-cabinet-reshuffle-2026-mohan-yadav-eyes-ministry/article-15391). As of the research date (11 September 2026) no such reshuffle has occurred and both ministers' Wikipedia pages still show their December 2023 portfolios, but Vijayvargiya's and Patel's portfolios should be treated as most at near-term risk of change and reconfirmed before any high-stakes outreach. CM Mohan Yadav personally retains General Administration, Home, Jail, and Industrial Policy and Investment Promotion, meaning — as in Bihar, Jharkhand, and Tamil Nadu — the Chief Minister personally controls the police/enforcement chain, a recurring structural pattern across states in this document set. The DGP is Kailash Makwana, IPS (1988-batch), appointed 1 December 2024 by Home Department order dated 23 November 2024, originally due to retire December 2025 but extended to December 2026 under Supreme Court two-year-minimum-tenure guidelines; a fresh 11 September 2026 re-check found no replacement, resignation, or transfer, so his tenure through December 2026 stands reconfirmed.

assam.political_context: Assam held Legislative Assembly elections in 2026, and Himanta Biswa Sarma (BJP) was returned for a second term as Chief Minister, with the new (Second Sarma) ministry sworn in on 12 May 2026 in an initial CM-plus-four ceremony, followed by a full cabinet expansion of 12 additional ministers on 5 June 2026, bringing the council of ministers to 17 (14 BJP, 2 AGP, 1 BPF). CM Himanta Biswa Sarma personally holds an unusually concentrated set of portfolios: Home (except Prisons, Home Guards), Personnel, Public Works (Buildings & National Highways), Public Works (Roads), and Medical Education & Research -- described in the source research as the most concentrated portfolio structure found across all states researched in that series, since it gives one office simultaneous control of enforcement (Home/Police), road engineering (both PWD wings), and medical education (relevant to trauma-care training). Other cabinet portfolios relevant to road safety are Transport & Welfare of Bodoland (Charan Boro, BPF), Health & Family Welfare (Ashok Singhal, BJP), Revenue & Disaster Management (Keshab Mahanta, AGP), Panchayat & Rural Development / Implementation of Assam Accord / Excise / Border Protection & Development (Atul Bora, AGP), and Housing & Urban Affairs (Kaushik Rai, BJP); all five were re-verified in the 11 September 2026 pass against at least one non-Wikipedia source. Harmeet Singh, IPS (1992-batch, Assam-Meghalaya cadre) is DGP, having taken charge as acting DGP on 29 January 2025 and being formally promoted/confirmed effective 29 May 2025, after earlier serving as Guwahati Police Commissioner; he was actively re-checked for a 2026 transfer or successor and none was found, with directory snapshots dated 6 January 2026 and 16 March 2026 and a September 2026 press-meet report all consistent with him still holding the post. Assam's current district count is 35, re-checked in the verification pass and corroborated by multiple current (2026-dated) sources (Verified, Moderate Confidence, since no single authoritative Revenue Department gazette listing was checked directly). Courts relevant to road safety are Motor Accident Claims Tribunals (MACTs) for compensation and Judicial Magistrate courts for prosecutable offences; a search for a current (2025/2026) Gauhati High Court PIL specifically on road/bridge safety did not surface one -- the only identified case, a dismissal of a PIL over Maligaon Flyover construction safety, dates to 16 September 2023 and is now stale.

haryana.political_context: Nayab Singh Saini (BJP) has served as Chief Minister of Haryana since March 2024 and was returned to office after the October 2024 Haryana Legislative Assembly election, with cabinet portfolios allocated on 21 October 2024. CM Saini personally holds 12 portfolios, including Home, Finance, Planning, Excise & Taxation, Town & Country Planning, Urban Estates, Housing, Criminal Investigation, and Law & Legislative — a centralisation pattern similar to several other states in this research series (CM personally holding Home plus land-use/urban portfolios), though PWD and Transport sit with separate ministers here, unlike Assam. The full October 2024 cabinet portfolio list was independently cross-checked against a full Wikipedia cabinet-list page (Second Saini ministry) plus individual minister pages, and no reshuffle since October 2024 was found across three independent search/fetch angles. On policing, Ajay Singhal, IPS (1992-batch), took charge as Haryana DGP on 1 January 2026, with a guaranteed minimum two-year tenure under the 2006 Prakash Singh Supreme Court judgment and a natural retirement date of 31 October 2028; he succeeded O. P. Singh, who had held interim charge after predecessor Shatrujeet Singh Kapur went on leave while named as an accused in an IPS officer's suicide case. Re-verification on 11 September 2026 against the most recent Haryana IPS reshuffle (26 June 2026) confirmed Singhal remains DGP, having received only an additional charge as Chairman/MD of the Haryana Police Housing Corporation.

telangana.political_context: A. Revanth Reddy (Congress) has served as Chief Minister of Telangana since 7 December 2023, heading the state's first Congress government since Telangana's 2014 creation. Cabinet portfolios were allocated shortly after, with the CM personally retaining Municipal Administration & Urban Development (MAUD), General Administration, and Law & Order (i.e., Home/Police), plus all unallocated portfolios — meaning the same office controls both statewide enforcement and Hyderabad's urban civic administration (GHMC oversight sits under MAUD), a pattern also seen in Bihar, Jharkhand, Tamil Nadu, Assam, and Haryana. The full December 2023 cabinet portfolio list rests primarily on a single South First article, with Komatireddy Venkat Reddy (Roads and Buildings), Ponnam Prabhakar (Transport), and N. Uttam Kumar Reddy (Irrigation and CAD, Food and Civil Supplies — confirmed NOT Home Minister despite an initially ambiguous source reference) independently cross-checked against Wikipedia. C. V. Anand, IPS, took charge as Telangana DGP on 1 May 2026 and, notably for CrashFree India, immediately announced plans for a dedicated Traffic Management and Road Safety Bureau (TG-TMARS) for consistent statewide enforcement; as of the most recent source found (27 August 2026), TG-TMARS remains not operational, with Chief Secretary Sanjay Jaju still directing officials to build a common traffic-data platform roughly four months after the announcement. Anand previously served as Hyderabad Police Commissioner (2024-2025), succeeded in that role by V. C. Sajjanar, IPS, who assumed charge 30 September 2025 and remains Hyderabad Police Commissioner as of this audit (September 2026), with no reports of a subsequent transfer found.

maharashtra.political_context: Maharashtra is governed by the Mahayuti coalition (BJP + Shiv Sena-Shinde + NCP-Ajit Pawar faction, the last now led by Sunetra Pawar following Ajit Pawar's death in January 2026), formed after the November 2024 state assembly election. Devendra Fadnavis (BJP) became Chief Minister for a third time on 5 December 2024 and personally holds Home Affairs, Finance, Planning, Energy, Law & Judiciary, General Administration, and Information & Public Relations -- Home gives him direct control of the state police (and therefore Highway Police oversight), consistent with the pattern seen in other states of the CM personally retaining Home. Deputy CM Eknath Shinde (Shiv Sena) holds Urban Development, Housing, and Public Works (including Public Undertakings), and is ex officio Chairman of both the MMRDA Authority and MSRDC by virtue of the Urban Development portfolio. Deputy CM Ajit Pawar (NCP), who had held Finance, Planning, and State Excise among other portfolios, died on 28 January 2026 in an air-charter crash near Baramati Airport along with four others on board; Finance and Planning passed directly to CM Fadnavis on the day of his death, and his widow Sunetra Pawar succeeded him as Deputy CM three days later (31 January 2026), retaining State Excise, Sports & Youth Welfare, and Minority Development and Aukaf, but not Finance or Planning. PWD itself is split between a 'Public Works (excluding Public Undertakings)' wing held by a dedicated PWD minister (Shivendrasinhraje Bhosale) and a 'Public Works (including Public Undertakings)' wing nominally under Shinde -- a jurisdictional split distinctive to Maharashtra among the states researched so far. The Chief Secretary is Rajesh Aggarwal, appointed 1 December 2025.

governance_bodies.meeting_frequency: 22-member body: Transport Commissioner (member-secretary), PWD and Transport ministers, state officials from Home/Transport/BMC, plus 8 special invitees (public health, urban development, media). Biannual meetings are mandatory by regulation. STANDOUT FINDING -- RECONFIRMED AND UPDATED this pass (11 Sept 2026): the Council has still not met since 4 April 2023. A newer, independent source (newsdrum.in, published 14 June 2026) directly reconfirms the gap and updates the figure: "more than 38 months have passed without a single meeting," and quotes Transport Minister Pratap Sarnaik promising the Council would finally convene "in the first week of July [2026]," contingent on completion of a three-year road safety plan. A second search attempt (for evidence the promised July 2026 meeting actually occurred) found no confirming report either way. Since inception in 2015, meetings should have occurred biannually under the mandatory schedule; only 12 were actually held per the original report. A retired RTO official is quoted characterizing the gap as "administrative apathy"; officials cited election code-of-conduct restrictions, though other government committees continued meeting during the same period. Experts quoted warn that without regular review, Maharashtra cannot meet its 50% road-fatality-reduction target by 2030. The state recorded 36,567 fatalities and 83,820 accidents between January 2023 and April 2025. Separately, a Maharashtra Transport Commissioner circular (11 Feb 2026) declared 2026 the "Save Two-Wheeler Riders & Pedestrians Year" following a state-level road-safety review meeting held 28-29 January 2026 -- but this departmental review meeting is distinct from, and does not substitute for, a statutory State Road Safety Council meeting, and no source ties it to the Council specifically. This remains the single most concrete documented road-safety-governance failure found across all nine states researched to date, and if anything is more acute than originally documented (38 months and counting, not "nearly two years").

gujarat.political_context: Bhupendra Patel (BJP) has been Chief Minister of Gujarat since 13 September 2021, re-elected for a second term on 12 December 2022. Unusually compared to other states researched, CM Patel personally holds the roads-engineering portfolio himself — General Administration, Administrative Reforms & Training, Planning, and Roads and Buildings and Capital Projects — publicly announcing large project allocations under his own name (e.g., ₹7,737 crore for 124 projects, October 2025) rather than delegating roads/PWD to a separate minister. Deputy CM Harsh Sanghavi (BJP), Deputy CM since 17 October 2025, holds Home Affairs, Law and Justice, Tourism, Industries, MSME & Civil Aviation, plus (continuing from his earlier appointment of 16 September 2021) Transport, Sports/Youth Affairs/Cultural Activities, Excise & Prohibition, and Border Security & Prisons — uniquely combining Home (police) and Transport, the two levers most directly relevant to enforcement and vehicle regulation, in one office. Other road-relevant ministers include Kanubhai Desai (Finance, Urban Development, Urban Housing) and Kunvarjibhai Bavaliya (Labour, Skill Development & Employment, Rural Development). Chief Secretary Manoj Kumar Das (1990-batch IAS) took charge effective 31 October 2025, succeeding Pankaj Joshi on his superannuation, with a tenure slated through December 2026. A historical note: Jaydrathsinh Parmar held a State Minister of Roads and Buildings role from 2012–2017, and a separate Agriculture/Panchayat/Environment portfolio Dec 2017–Sept 2021, but does not currently hold any R&B portfolio.

governance_bodies.name: Gujarat Road Safety Authority (GRSA)
governance_bodies.mandate: A dedicated statutory Authority — the most institutionally developed road-safety-specific body found across all nine states researched to date alongside Karnataka's KSRSA. Established under the Gujarat Road Safety Authority Act, 2018, operating under the Gujarat Road Safety Rules and Orders, 2020. Implements road safety across four pillars: enforcement, road engineering, emergency care, and education.
governance_bodies.roads_owned: Not a road-owning body — a coordinating/implementing safety authority operating across road types.
governance_bodies.hierarchy: Chief Road Safety Commissioner at the operational head — per Section 3(4) of the Gujarat Road Safety Authority Act, 2018, this statutory post is "the Chief Executive Officer of the Authority" and "head of the staff of the Authority" — supported by a Joint Commissioner and Chief Enforcement Officer. The Authority itself has 14 statutory members drawn from Transport, Home, Health, Education, R&B, law enforcement, transport corporations, municipal administration, highway authorities, automobile associations, and two nominated road-safety experts. An Executive Committee, chaired by the Additional Chief Secretary (Transport), meets bimonthly. The broader Authority and a State Road Safety Council operate under the chairmanship of the Transport Minister (currently Deputy CM Harsh Sanghavi, by virtue of his Transport portfolio), meeting biannually. Re-verified 11 Sept 2026: statutory title corrected from "Road Safety Commissioner" to "Chief Road Safety Commissioner" per the Act text itself, upgrading the earlier single-secondary-source characterization.

uttar_pradesh.political_context: Yogi Adityanath (BJP) has been Chief Minister of Uttar Pradesh since 19 March 2017, now in his second term following the 2022 election, and remained CM through the state's constitutional Seventh Schedule-driven governance structure at least as recently as 25 September 2026, confirmed via a same-day report of his attendance at the Uttar Pradesh International Trade Show (UPITS-2026) inauguration. His personal portfolio concentration remains the single most extensive found across states researched to date: he directly holds Home, Public Works Department (PWD, Cabinet-rank charge vacant since June 2024), Law, General Administration, Cabinet Affairs, Information & Public Relations, Housing, Revenue, Mining & Geology, Institutional Finance, Planning, Civil Aviation, Food Safety & Drug Administration and other unallotted departments -- 25+ departments overall (Verified, The Print). PWD's Cabinet-rank charge history: Keshav Prasad Maurya (now Deputy CM) held it 19 March 2017 - 25 March 2022, succeeded by Cabinet Minister Jitin Prasada (25 March 2022 - 11 June 2024), who resigned on becoming a Union Minister of State; no Cabinet-rank successor has been appointed since. Minister of State Brijesh Singh (BJP MLA, Deoband) has held the PWD MoS portfolio continuously since 25 March 2022 and is the closest thing to a day-to-day ministerial face for PWD, though independent 2026-dated confirmation of his continuation was limited to lower-tier regional outlets (see flags). The two Deputy CMs -- Keshav Prasad Maurya (Rural Development since 25 March 2022; Food Processing Industries since 19 March 2017) and Brajesh Pathak (Health & Family Welfare, Medical Education since 25 March 2022) -- were reconfirmed in place through the UP cabinet's second expansion on 10 May 2026 (six new ministers inducted, taking the ministry to the constitutional ceiling of 60), a reshuffle that added Bhupendra Chaudhary and Manoj Pandey as Cabinet Ministers and four MLAs as Ministers of State without altering the Transport, PWD or Deputy CM portfolios. The Transport Minister is Daya Shankar Singh, Minister of State (Independent Charge) since 25 March 2022, reconfirmed still in post as recently as 23 September 2026 (Free Press Journal) and notable among all UP political figures for the most consistent, dated, road-safety-specific track record found in this pass -- spanning a December 2025 CM-chaired road-safety review, the January 2026 statewide 'Road Safety Month', and an April 2026 PPP-based bus-station-safety modernisation programme. Chief Secretary Shashi Prakash Goyal (1989-batch IAS, UP cadre) took charge on 1 August 2025, succeeding Manoj Kumar Singh, and is slated to serve until his own retirement in January 2027; no successor or 2026 transfer was found in this pass (absence-of-contradiction only). Rajeev Krishna (1991-batch IPS) was confirmed as UP's first permanent DGP since 2022 on 31 May 2026, ending an extended acting period, and remained active in the role as of 21 September 2026 (Indian Masterminds, addressing new recruits). Below the political layer, a September 2025 IPS reshuffle installed A. Satish Ganesh (1996-batch IPS) as ADG, Traffic & Road Safety Directorate, and he remained in that post and publicly engaged on road-safety technology as of August 2026 (Safe City & Intelligent Mobility India Summit). A parallel September 2025 IAS reshuffle resolved a standing research gap from the prior file: Deepak Kumar, IAS, was named Infrastructure & Industrial Development Commissioner (IIDC) and concurrently CEO of the Uttar Pradesh Expressways Industrial Development Authority (UPEIDA) -- the body that builds and operates UP's high-speed expressway network (Purvanchal, Bundelkhand, Ganga, Agra-Lucknow) where a large share of the state's highest-severity crashes occur -- resolving the prior file's 'UPEIDA CEO unconfirmed' flag. In a further structural shift reported in mid-2026, UPEIDA itself was moved out of the Industrial Development Minister's (Nand Gopal Gupta's) nominal oversight and placed directly under the Chief Minister's Infrastructure Development Department (The Print), meaning expressway safety and construction-quality accountability now runs more directly through the CM's office and IIDC Deepak Kumar than through the Industries portfolio. On the bureaucratic side, Sanjay Prasad (1995-batch IAS) was promoted to Additional Chief Secretary, Home & Confidential in January 2026, making him the senior-most bureaucrat under the CM's own Home portfolio and therefore a central node for traffic-enforcement policy and budget. On the opposition side, Mata Prasad Pandey (Samajwadi Party) has been Leader of the Opposition in the UP Legislative Assembly since 28 July 2024 (PRS Legislative Research), though no road-safety-specific statement by him was found in this pass; Samajwadi Party national president and former CM Akhilesh Yadav has instead been the most visible and recurring critical voice on road/expressway safety, most recently in a 17 September 2026 statement (The Print) alleging systemic construction-quality failures across the Purvanchal, Bundelkhand and Ganga Expressways. Separately, Congress Legislature Party leader Aradhana Mishra 'Mona' delivered a detailed, data-heavy road-safety intervention in the UP Assembly on 13 February 2026 (IANS), citing ~45,000 annual accidents and over 24,000 deaths and demanding engineering audits of black spots, statewide ITMS rollout and a traffic-police staffing fix (state has roughly 9,000 traffic personnel against an estimated requirement of 30,000, per her own figures as reported). As in the other pilot states, India's constitutional Seventh Schedule splits road-related subjects across the Union and State Lists, and because roads, transport and police sit substantially on the State List, Uttar Pradesh's state government and its departments -- not the Union -- are the primary point of leverage for almost all road-safety interventions CrashFree India will pursue in the state, with the Union mattering mainly for National Highway stretches, PMGSY funding rules and the Motor Vehicles Act framework.

governance_bodies.name: Home Department / Uttar Pradesh Police (incl. Traffic Directorate)
governance_bodies.mandate: Overall command of law and order and traffic enforcement statewide, under the Home Department (portfolio held directly by CM Yogi Adityanath).
governance_bodies.roads_owned: None -- an enforcement body, not a road-owning one. Enforcement decisions (checkpoints, helmet drives, ITMS camera siting) are made at ADG (Traffic & Road Safety) and district SSP/SP level; infrastructure decisions that police influence but don't own require joint sign-off with the road-owning department.
governance_bodies.hierarchy: Director General of Police (DGP) heads UP Police. An Additional Director General of Police heads the Traffic & Road Safety Directorate statewide. Below the state level, UP Police is organised into 8 police zones (each headed by an ADG), 18 police ranges (each headed by an IG or DIG), and district units headed by a Senior Superintendent of Police (SSP) or Superintendent of Police (SP); each district is further divided into police circles headed by a Circle Officer (CO, DSP rank; a circle typically comprises 3-5 police stations), and circles into Thanas (police stations) headed by Inspectors/Sub-Inspectors. Several large cities (Lucknow, Kanpur, Varanasi, Agra, Ghaziabad, Prayagraj, Noida, and others) have been converted to the Police Commissionerate system, under which a Commissioner of Police holds magisterial as well as policing powers, distinct from the district-SSP model used elsewhere in the state.
governance_bodies.subordinate_bodies: Traffic & Road Safety Directorate; State Disaster Response Force (SDRF), organisationally a Police unit rather than reporting to UPSDMA directly (see UPSDMA entry); UP Police Academy and training establishments.

governance_bodies.name: Panchayati Raj Institutions (PRIs), Uttar Pradesh
governance_bodies.mandate: Rural local self-government under the United Provinces Panchayat Raj Act, 1947 (Gram Panchayats) and the Uttar Pradesh Kshettra Panchayats and Zila Panchayats Adhiniyam, 1961 (the two higher tiers), both amended to conform to the 73rd Constitutional Amendment.
governance_bodies.roads_owned: Very limited -- Gram Panchayats can maintain purely internal village streets/drains where GP funds (15th Finance Commission grants, MGNREGA convergence, own tax revenue) allow; cannot independently execute PMGSY-scale road construction, which the state government (via UPRRDA) retains responsibility for even on roads serving Panchayat areas.
governance_bodies.hierarchy: Three tiers: Gram Panchayat (village level), Kshettra Panchayat (block level; historically called Kshetra Samiti), and Zila Panchayat (district level; historically called Zila Parishad). The state's own Panchayati Raj Department page lists 75 Zila Panchayats as the district-level count, consistent with UP's 75 administrative districts.
governance_bodies.subordinate_bodies: Elected political heads: Pradhan (Gram Panchayat), Block Pramukh (Kshettra Panchayat), Adhyaksha (Zila Panchayat). Administrative/executive counterparts report up the state administrative line (Panchayati Raj Department -> Director -> district cadre), not to the elected head, mirroring the pattern documented in other states.

governance_bodies.name: Urban Development Department and Urban Local Bodies (Nagar Nigams, Nagar Palika Parishads, Nagar Panchayats) and Development Authorities
governance_bodies.mandate: The Urban Development Department sets urban policy and oversees Urban Local Bodies (ULBs), constituted under the Uttar Pradesh Municipal Corporations Act, 1959 (for Nagar Nigams/Municipal Corporations) and the UP Municipalities Act, 1916 (for Nagar Palika Parishads/Nagar Panchayats); separately, Development Authorities (constituted under the UP Urban Planning and Development Act, 1973) handle land-use planning and new-area development for major cities -- e.g. Lucknow Development Authority (LDA), Kanpur Development Authority (KDA, formed 1973), Agra Development Authority (ADA), Varanasi Development Authority (VDA), Ghaziabad Development Authority (GDA), and the separately statute-constituted New Okhla Industrial Development Authority (NOIDA) and Greater Noida Industrial Development Authority (GNIDA), both under the UP Industrial Area Development Act 1976 (the same Act underpinning UPEIDA).
governance_bodies.roads_owned: Municipal roads within ULB limits: 17 Municipal Corporations (Nagar Nigams) including Lucknow, Kanpur, Varanasi, Agra, Ghaziabad and Prayagraj, plus Municipal Councils and Nagar Panchayats statewide, own and maintain roads within their limits; Development Authorities own/plan roads within their development-scheme areas until handover to the relevant ULB, a handover that (per the pattern documented in other states' development-authority relationships) is frequently delayed.
governance_bodies.hierarchy: Cabinet Minister A.K. Sharma (Urban Development & Energy) -> Principal Secretary, Urban Development -> Directorate of Local Bodies (for Nagar Nigams/Councils/Panchayats) and separately the individual Development Authorities (each with its own Vice-Chairman/CEO, typically an IAS officer, and a Chairman who in some cases is the Divisional Commissioner or another senior state appointee). Each Nagar Nigam has an elected wing (Mayor plus ward councillors) and a separate administrative wing headed by a Municipal Commissioner (an IAS or senior PCS officer appointed by the state government, not answerable to the elected Mayor for personnel matters) -- e.g. Lucknow Municipal Corporation (LMC) is headed administratively by an IAS-rank Municipal Commissioner with full executive powers, operating alongside but organisationally separate from LDA.
governance_bodies.subordinate_bodies: Directorate of Local Bodies; State Urban Development Agency (SUDA); Uttar Pradesh Jal Nigam (water/sewerage); the individual Development Authorities (LDA, KDA, ADA, VDA, GDA, NOIDA, GNIDA, and others for each major city) function as parastatal bodies distinct from -- and sometimes overlapping in jurisdiction with -- the Nagar Nigams.

governance_bodies.performance_issues: Overlap risk: for a single street in a city like Lucknow or Noida, the Nagar Nigam may own the carriageway/footpath, a Development Authority (LDA, NOIDA, GNIDA) may control an arterial stretch or land-use/setback rules along the frontage, and city Traffic Police controls signalling/enforcement -- a single 'fix this junction' request can require sign-off from three or more institutions, mirroring the pattern documented in Bihar's Patna case. UP's Development Authority landscape is unusually large and fragmented (a distinct authority per major city, plus NOIDA/GNIDA as separate industrial-development authorities), which this pass judges likely increases -- though does not have direct quantified evidence for -- this coordination burden relative to states with fewer or more consolidated development authorities.

governance_bodies.name: Uttar Pradesh State Disaster Management Authority (UPSDMA)
governance_bodies.mandate: Constituted under the Disaster Management Act, 2005 (applied to UP via the state's own disaster-management framework) as the apex state body for disaster policy, planning and coordination; institutionally linked to mass-casualty response (major bus/truck crashes, pile-ups, bridge collapses) rather than routine single-vehicle crash response, which sits with Police/Health.
governance_bodies.roads_owned: None.
governance_bodies.hierarchy: Chairman: Chief Minister Yogi Adityanath (by statute, the standard pattern for State Disaster Management Authorities under the Disaster Management Act 2005). Vice-Chairman: Lt. Gen. Yogendra Dimri, AVSM (since on or about 15 January 2024, succeeding Lt. Gen. Ravindra Pratap Sahi, AVSM, who served 2018-2024). A CEO/Member-Secretary post exists per the Authority's standard organisational documents, but a specific current named officeholder was not confirmed via a working primary source in this pass (the Authority's own website returned repeated server errors).
governance_bodies.subordinate_bodies: State Disaster Response Force (SDRF) -- notably, UP's SDRF is organised as a unit of UP Police (headquartered in Lucknow, with Regional Response Centres across Western, Central and Eastern zones covering Bareilly/Moradabad, Lucknow/Etawah, and Ayodhya/Prayagraj/Mirzapur/Varanasi/Gorakhpur respectively) rather than reporting directly to UPSDMA -- a structural point worth flagging since it differs from a model where SDRF reports through the disaster-management authority itself. UP Police's own SDRF page explicitly lists "Road Accident" and "Train Accident" among the disaster categories SDRF responds to, alongside flood, earthquake, fire, and chemical/biological/radiological/nuclear incidents; Aapda Mitra (community-volunteer first-responder training) also operates in the state as part of the national programme.

governance_bodies.decision_making_power: The Management Committee controls Fund expenditure. Funding sources: 50% of the amount collected in any financial year through compounding of offences under the Motor Vehicles Act by the Police and Transport Departments is deposited into the Fund via budget provision in the following financial year, plus financial contributions from the UP Government or Government of India. Permitted uses: road signage and traffic signals; accident-data management systems; ambulance services; corrective measures at accident-prone locations (black spots); traffic-enforcement equipment; driving-test tracks; vehicle-inspection facilities; and traffic-safety-education programmes. Explicit restriction: Fund monies may never be placed in fixed-deposit schemes or used to extend loans.

key_individuals.priorities_and_interests: His documented public record centers on rural transport access and connectivity growth -- the Mukhyamantri Gram Parivahan Yojana (linking 12,200 villages), the zero-commission 'Bharat Taxi' rural bus model, and the bus-station PPP -- explicitly framed around the state government's $1-trillion-economy-by-2030 / $6-trillion-by-2047 target (Business Standard interview, Jul 2026), with road safety folded in as one component of that growth agenda rather than pursued as a freestanding goal. Politically, as a second-term MLA holding a sub-Cabinet (Independent Charge) portfolio, sustained visibility on a popular, low-controversy issue is a plausible way to build standing within the BJP legislature party. bihar.political_context: Bihar held Legislative Assembly elections in November 2025, and the state's government changed hands in April–May 2026: Nitish Kumar's uninterrupted run as Chief Minister ended on 15 April 2026, and Samrat Choudhary (BJP) was sworn in as the 24th Chief Minister the same day, with the full cabinet reshuffled and portfolios allocated on 7–8 May 2026. As of the most recent verification (9 September 2026), Samrat Choudhary was confirmed still actively functioning as CM through contemporaneous press coverage of his public appearances (felicitating students, attending public events). Under the 8 May 2026 portfolio allocation, the CM retains Home, General Administration, Vigilance, Election, Civil Aviation and unallocated departments; Deputy CM Vijay Kumar Chaudhary holds Water Resources & Parliamentary Affairs; Deputy CM Bijendra Prasad Yadav holds Finance & Commercial Taxes; Road Construction went to Kumar Shailendra; and Energy went to Shailesh Kumar ("Bulo Mandal"). This is a structural change with direct road-safety consequences: the Transport Minister (now Damodar Rawat), the Road Construction Minister (now Kumar Shailendra), and both Deputy Chief Ministers are all different people than a year ago, meaning most of Bihar's road-safety-relevant political leadership is newly in role and has, by definition, no track record yet in its current position. Underlying this political layer, India's constitutional Seventh Schedule splits road-related subjects across the Union and State Lists, and because roads, transport and police all sit substantially on the State List (with the Union retaining National Highways, the overarching Motor Vehicles Act framework, and centrally sponsored schemes like PMGSY), Bihar's state government and its departments are the primary point of leverage for almost all road-safety interventions CrashFree India will pursue — the Union government matters mainly for NH stretches, PMGSY funding rules, and the national legal framework. Additionally, this pass resolved a previously unnamed gap: the 7–8 May 2026 cabinet expansion allocated the Health portfolio to Nishant Kumar, son of former CM and JD(U) national president Nitish Kumar, his first ministerial appointment (LatestLY, Republic World, Daily Pioneer) — relevant background given JD(U)’s continuing weight in the coalition despite Nitish Kumar himself now sitting in the Rajya Sabha.

governance_bodies.name: Panchayati Raj Institutions (PRIs)
governance_bodies.mandate: Rural local self-government under the Bihar Panchayat Raj Act, 2006, implementing the 73rd Constitutional Amendment.
governance_bodies.roads_owned: Very limited — Gram Panchayats can maintain purely internal village streets/drains where GP funds (15th Finance Commission grants, MGNREGA convergence, own tax revenue) allow; cannot independently execute PMGSY/MMGSY-scale road construction.
governance_bodies.hierarchy: Three tiers: Gram Panchayat (GP) at village level, Panchayat Samiti at Block level, and Zila Parishad at District level — at present 8,053 Gram Panchayats, 533 Panchayat Samitis and 38 Zila Parishads are functional, with Gram Panchayats divided into roughly 1.15 lakh wards. A Gram Kachahry (village-level dispute-resolution body) exists at each GP; a Ward Sabha exists at each ward under the Ward Member, alongside the Gram Sabha at GP level.
governance_bodies.subordinate_bodies: Elected political heads: Mukhiya (GP), Pramukh (Panchayat Samiti), Adhyaksha (Zila Parishad). Administrative/executive counterparts: Panchayat Secretary (GP), BDO-cum-Executive Officer (Panchayat Samiti), and Deputy Development Commissioner-cum-CEO (Zila Parishad) — reporting up the state administrative line (Panchayati Raj Department → Director → district BDO/DDC cadre), not to the elected head.
governance_bodies.decision_making_power: A Gram Panchayat may impose a yearly tax on occupants of holdings, and on professions, trades, callings and employment carried on within its jurisdiction, subject to State Government approval of the maximum tax rate (Section 27, BPRA 2006); the State Government retains rule-making power (Section 146) and the power to issue model regulations and inquire into Panchayat affairs (Sections 150 and 152). Every Gram Panchayat must prepare a development plan annually and submit it to the Panchayat Samiti (Sections 166–167).
governance_bodies.data_role: PRIs have a formally recognised awareness/participation role in road safety — the 2020 amendment to Bihar's Road Safety Council Rules explicitly tasks the Transport Department's coordination committee with ensuring "active participation of Panchayati Raj Institutions, Urban Local Bodies and NGOs in road safety awareness programmes" — distinct from an engineering role.
governance_bodies.performance_issues: The state government intimated in Feb. 2005, based on department resolutions from September 2001, that functions of 20 departments had been devolved to PRIs — but a CAG review found that while activity mapping had been done, actual transfer of functions, functionaries and funds to PRIs by these departments had not fully materialised — a documented, audited gap between paper devolution and real administrative control.
governance_bodies.meeting_frequency: Annual development-plan submission cycle (Sections 166–167, BPRA 2006); Gram Sabha/Ward Sabha meetings for local matters.

subordinates_parsed.text: Elected political heads: Mukhiya (GP), Pramukh (Panchayat Samiti), Adhyaksha (Zila Parishad). Administrative/executive counterparts: Panchayat Secretary (GP), BDO-cum-Executive Officer (Panchayat Samiti), and Deputy Development Commissioner-cum-CEO (Zila Parishad) — reporting up the state administrative line (Panchayati Raj Department → Director → district BDO/DDC cadre), not to the elected head.

governance_bodies.name: Home Department / Bihar Police (incl. Traffic Police)
governance_bodies.mandate: Overall command of law and order and traffic enforcement statewide, under the Home Department (headed politically by the Chief Minister, who traditionally also holds the Home portfolio in Bihar).
governance_bodies.roads_owned: None — an enforcement body, not a road-owning one. Enforcement decisions (checkpoint locations, helmet/seatbelt drives, drunk-driving campaigns) are made at ADG (Traffic) and district SP level; infrastructure decisions that police influence but don't own (camera placement, signal timing, physical traffic-calming) require joint sign-off with the Transport Department and/or the road-owning engineering department.
governance_bodies.hierarchy: Director General of Police (DGP) heads Bihar Police. An Additional Director General of Police (ADG), Traffic heads traffic policing statewide; district-level traffic enforcement is typically headed by an SP (Traffic) in major cities (e.g., Patna) or handled by the general district SP/SSP elsewhere, with Traffic DSPs and Traffic Inspectors/Sub-Inspectors at the operational level. Bihar has 43 Police Districts (headed by SP/SSP) and 853 Police Stations; a Police District is divided into Police Subdivisions headed by a DSP. Patna and other large cities have designated City SPs (e.g., SP City East/West) separate from rural SPs, plus a dedicated SP (Traffic), Patna.
governance_bodies.subordinate_bodies: Crime Investigation Department (CID) for serious/fatal hit-and-run or negligence cases; Economic Offences Unit; Bihar Police Academy and Constable Training School/Military Police training centres.

governance_bodies.name: Urban Development & Housing Department (UDHD) and Urban Local Bodies
governance_bodies.mandate: UDHD sets urban policy; its principal implementing arm for infrastructure is BUIDCO (Bihar Urban Infrastructure Development Corporation), established 2009 under the Companies Act 1956, functioning as the apex body for planning, coordination and implementation of urban development projects (water supply, sewerage, urban transport, housing, solid waste management).
governance_bodies.roads_owned: Municipal roads within Urban Local Body limits (Nagar Nigams/Municipal Corporations, Nagar Parishads/Municipal Councils, Nagar Panchayats) under the Bihar Municipal Act, 2007 — as of April 2026 there were 264 Urban Local Bodies in the state. Patna Municipal Corporation (PMC, established 1952) handles municipal roads, drains, streetlights within Patna.
governance_bodies.hierarchy: Each ULB has an elected wing (Mayor for Corporations, Chairperson for Councils, President for Nagar Panchayats, plus ward councillors) and a separate administrative wing; day-to-day execution runs through a Municipal Commissioner (Corporations) or Executive Officer (Councils/Nagar Panchayats), state cadre officers not directly under the elected Mayor's control for personnel matters.
governance_bodies.subordinate_bodies: BUIDCO; the Patna Metropolitan Area Authority (PMAA) — the current metropolitan planning body, constituted under the Bihar Urban Planning & Development Act, 2012, as successor to the defunct Patna Regional Development Authority (PRDA, established 1979, dissolved 2007 when the Bihar Municipal Act, 2007 repealed its enabling legislation).

karnataka.political_context: Siddaramaiah resigned as Chief Minister on 28 May 2026 and D. K. Shivakumar was sworn in as the 18th Chief Minister of Karnataka on 3 June 2026, with G. Parameshwara as Deputy CM (Revenue, Youth Empowerment and Sports), under an internal Congress power-sharing arrangement whose exact terms were never formally announced. Portfolios were allocated on 4 June 2026 and reshuffled again on 27 August 2026 when the cabinet was expanded. As of Shivakumar's 100th day in office (10 September 2026, an event his predecessor Siddaramaiah himself inaugurated and publicly endorsed) he remains Chief Minister with no rotation back to Siddaramaiah having occurred, though persistent speculation about a power-sharing 'rotation' understanding means this should be re-checked before any future use of this document. Priyank Kharge became Home Minister (excluding Intelligence, which the CM retains) from the June 2026 reshuffle, with a strongly technology/digital-policing-focused agenda; Byrathi Suresh became Transport Minister, succeeding Ramalinga Reddy (who moved to Major and Medium Irrigation/Water Resources, then to Forest, Ecology and Environment on 13 August 2026 after briefly resigning over being denied the Bengaluru Development portfolio); and Satish Jarkiholi retained Public Works through the August 2026 reshuffle. The single most significant new development remains that, on 9 September 2026, the Enforcement Directorate conducted money-laundering raids at roughly 18-21 locations linked to PWD Minister Satish Jarkiholi, including his Bengaluru residence and properties tied to his MP daughter Priyanka Jarkiholi and other relatives/associates, seizing roughly Rs 3.3 crore in unaccounted cash; Chief Minister Shivakumar publicly called the raids 'politically motivated', and as of the most recent reporting located (13 September 2026) Jarkiholi remains PWD Minister with no resignation or removal reported — this is an active, fast-moving situation that could affect the stability of the PWD ministerial relationship on short notice, and no news dated after 13 September 2026 could be located despite a direct search. A second significant thread, newly surfaced in this pass, is genuine contradictory sourcing over who currently holds the state's ADGP Traffic and Road Safety post: prior reporting names both R. Hithendra (additional charge, reported June 2025) and Alok Kumar (continuously from June 2023 until his own transfer to ADGP Training around May 2026), and no confirmed successor to Alok Kumar in that specific post was located — CrashFree India should confirm this post's current holder directly before any outreach premised on it. Separately, Bengaluru's Joint Commissioner of Police (Traffic) changed hands in July 2025, from M. N. Anucheth (transferred to DIG, Recruitment) to Karthik Reddy, who has publicly framed his own mandate explicitly around improving road safety and traffic management — CrashFree India's working-level Bengaluru traffic-enforcement contact should be updated accordingly. Any reference to 'Transport Minister Ramalinga Reddy,' 'CM Siddaramaiah,' or 'Joint CP Traffic M. N. Anucheth' is now historically relevant only, not a current contact.

governance_bodies.performance_issues: Elections to Karnataka's Zilla Panchayats and Taluk Panchayats have not been held since 2020-21; the state government has instead appointed administrators to run these bodies for over five years. In December 2025 the Union Ministry of Panchayati Raj confirmed to the Lok Sabha it had withheld Rs. 1,279 crore in 15th Finance Commission grants to Karnataka specifically because of this non-conduct of elections. UPDATED in this 25 Sept 2026 audit pass: the Gram Panchayat tier has, in the interim, also lapsed into the same position — Gram Panchayats were last elected in December 2020 and their five-year terms expired in December 2025, so Karnataka's rural local bodies are now unelected across all three tiers (Gram, Taluk and Zilla Panchayat), contrary to this document's own prior-pass inference that Gram Panchayats might still have 2021-elected leadership. On 11 September 2026 the Karnataka High Court recorded that ward formation and seat reservation had been completed for all 5,864 Gram Panchayats statewide and directed the State Election Commission to proceed with conducting the polls — a genuine, concrete procedural unlock, though no election date has yet been fixed and this HC order concerns Gram Panchayats specifically, not Zilla/Taluk Panchayats. For the two higher tiers, Deccan Herald (citing Minister Eshwar Khandre) continues to report a government target of holding 'all pending panchayat elections' by end of 2026, complicated by delimitation work in Vijayapura/Bagalkote and a separate reservation-process extension sought from the High Court; elections to all three tiers may now be conducted together. Verified — Moderate-High Confidence via Bar & Bench (11 Sept 2026 HC order) and Deccan Herald reporting current to September 2026.

governance_bodies.name: Greater Bengaluru Authority (GBA) and the five City Corporations
governance_bodies.mandate: Greater Bengaluru Governance Act, 2024 (Karnataka Act No. 36 of 2025) abolished the Bruhat Bengaluru Mahanagara Palike (BBMP) and the BBMP Act, 2020, effective 15 May 2025, and replaced them with a three-tier structure: GBA at the apex (chaired by the Chief Minister); five City Corporations (Bengaluru Central, North, South, East and West); and Ward Committees below that. Fully operationalised from 2 September 2025.
governance_bodies.roads_owned: Each of the five City Corporations is the formal owner/custodian of municipal roads, footpaths, drains and streetlights within its zone, exactly as BBMP was before it.
governance_bodies.hierarchy: GBA (chaired by CM Shivakumar, bringing together all state ministers, Bengaluru-area MPs/MLAs/MLCs, and once elected, the five corporations' Mayors) -> Five City Corporations, each headed (in the absence of an elected Mayor) by an appointed IAS Municipal Commissioner -> Ward Committees. Bengaluru's roughly 198 former BBMP wards were redrawn and expanded into 369 wards across the five corporations (63 Central, 72 North, 72 South, 50 East, 112 West).
governance_bodies.subordinate_bodies: Parastatal bodies coordinated under the GBA umbrella: BESCOM (electricity), BWSSB (water/sewerage), BMTC (city bus transport), BMRCL (metro rail); also Bengaluru Solid Waste Management Ltd.

key_individuals.name: Dr. G. (Gopalkrishna) Gururaj
key_individuals.role: Dean, Centre for Public Health, Department of Epidemiology; Head, WHO Collaborating Centre for Injury Prevention and Safety Promotion, NIMHANS, Bengaluru
key_individuals.priority: Technical/research partnership route
key_individuals.influence: Leads the single most institutionally credible road-safety research and technical-assistance body headquartered in Karnataka, with a working relationship with Bengaluru Traffic Police and international funders.
key_individuals.road_safety_relevance: Has led the Bangalore Road Safety and Injury Prevention Programme since 2007; worked with Indian ministries and state governments on road safety, alongside international work advising Oman, Egypt, Iran and Indonesia on national road-safety frameworks; two-decade documented publication record on Indian road-traffic-injury epidemiology.

track_record.text: His institute co-authored and released, with Bengaluru Traffic Police, Johns Hopkins International Injury Research Unit and Bloomberg Philanthropies, a joint drunk-driving assessment report, discussed at a NIMHANS symposium on human behavioural risk factors in road traffic injuries.

citation.label: Deccan Herald, 22 Dec 2023, 'Bengaluru symposium addresses human behavioral factors in road traffic injuries'

track_record.text: A peer-reviewed paper on 'passive drink driving' interventions in Bengaluru lists Gururaj as a co-author alongside Bengaluru Traffic Police and Karnataka CID co-authors and Johns Hopkins/Bloomberg partners — evidence the collaboration is still active into 2026.

NIMHANS' WHO Collaborating Centre launched a 'lay responder care' module — scene safety, hands-only CPR, bleeding control, basic fracture management — that had trained over 900 people, including roughly 110 police personnel, as of 2026.

citation.label: NIMHANS, WHO Collaborating Centre for Injury Prevention and Safety Promotion, nimhans.ac.in

key_individuals.frequency_of_engagement: Recurring, long-running institutional engagement rather than a one-off; no departure, retirement, or change in his NIMHANS/WHO Collaborating Centre role found as of September 2026.
key_individuals.background: DCP3 author; two-decade publication record on Indian road-traffic-injury epidemiology; WHO Collaborating Centre focus areas include road traffic injuries, traumatic brain injury, childhood injuries, workplace injuries, and violence/suicide prevention.
key_individuals.value_to_crashfree: Potentially the fastest way for CrashFree India to access credible Karnataka-specific crash and behavioural data; a technical partnership route, not a political one.
key_individuals.suggested_approach: Approach as a technical/research partner — propose a specific, narrow collaboration (e.g., a district or corridor this programme hasn't yet reached) rather than a general partnership pitch. Assessment (not fact): given the standing NIMHANS-Police-Johns Hopkins-Bloomberg partnership, a new NGO approaching Bengaluru independently may find the ground already occupied — the more useful ask may be how CrashFree India's model complements rather than duplicates this existing programme.
key_individuals.priorities_and_interests: His institution's stated priorities center on sustaining and expanding the WHO Collaborating Centre's mandate — international advisory work (Oman, Egypt, Iran, Indonesia), the long-running Johns Hopkins/Bloomberg Philanthropies partnership with Bengaluru Traffic Police, and continued grant-funded publication output, which are his career's institutional incentives as much as personal advocacy. The 2026 pivot toward training lay responders and police personnel in trauma first-response suggests a near-term programmatic priority on capacity-building/scale rather than new research alone. No documented tension with road safety — his institutional and personal incentives are already fully aligned with it by design, which is unusual among this list and worth noting explicitly rather than assuming.
key_individuals.caveats: No changes located; reconfirmed.

key_individuals.name: Prof. M. N. Sreehari
key_individuals.role: Long-serving traffic/transportation advisor associated with the Government of Karnataka; heads a private infrastructure/transport consultancy (CEO, Consortia of Infrastructure Engineers and Transportation Engineering Consultancy Services)
key_individuals.priority: Technical reviewer route
key_individuals.influence: One of the few people bridging four decades of continuous, hands-on Bengaluru traffic-engineering advisory work with an informal-advisor relationship to the state government.
key_individuals.road_safety_relevance: Has educated over 4.5 lakh road users on road safety; became an advisor to the Government of Karnataka on Traffic, Transportation and Infrastructure in 2004; has conducted road-safety audits on more than 25 National Highways and advised NHAI on road-safety initiatives.

track_record.text: Continues to be quoted and interviewed by local and national media (including a February 2026 video interview) offering engineering-led fixes for Bengaluru traffic problems, including commentary on the city's tunnel-road project.

citation.label: 101Reporters, Feb 2026, 'M N Sreehari talks on the condition of traffic in Bengaluru' (video interview)

key_individuals.frequency_of_engagement: Continuous since 2004; reconfirmed active in public commentary through February 2026, no evidence of a change in his informal-advisor status.
key_individuals.background: Over 42 years as a transportation-engineering professor and consultant; became Government of Karnataka advisor on Traffic, Transportation and Infrastructure in 2004.
key_individuals.value_to_crashfree: Useful as institutional memory and a possible technical reviewer for a specific corridor or junction, more than as a decision-maker.
key_individuals.suggested_approach: Not specified beyond his role as institutional memory/technical reviewer.
key_individuals.priorities_and_interests: His public statements consistently favour large infrastructure/engineering solutions (flyovers, tunnel roads, signal and audit fixes) over enforcement- or behaviour-change-led approaches — consistent with, though not provably driven by, his consultancy firms' commercial interest in infrastructure design and advisory contracts (inference, not a documented conflict). His institutional incentive as a 20-plus-year informal government advisor is likely to preserve continued relevance and visibility as Bengaluru's go-to traffic commentator. Not enough on record to say whether he sees CFI's likely behaviour-change/enforcement framing as complementary or competing with his engineering-first advocacy.
key_individuals.caveats: No changes located; reconfirmed.

jharkhand.political_context: Hemant Soren (Jharkhand Mukti Morcha, JMM) has led an INDIA-bloc coalition government (JMM + Congress + RJD) continuously since re-election in December 2024, following the JMM-led alliance's 56/81-seat win in the November 2024 Assembly election; he has served as Chief Minister since 4 July 2024 (having previously held the post 2019-2024 and briefly in 2013-2014) and as President of the JMM since 15 April 2025. This was reconfirmed current via the Jharkhand Transport Department's live official website during this verification pass (Hemant Soren — Wikipedia; Transport Department, Government of Jharkhand — live site). The cabinet sworn in with him has been largely stable since December 2024, with three significant recent disruptions: the Director General of Police post has changed hands three times in under two years (Anurag Gupta → Tadasha Mishra, acting → Tadasha Mishra, regular, the last change in late December 2025); Cabinet Minister Sudivya Kumar (JMM, Urban Development & Housing, Higher/Technical Education, Tourism, Sports & Youth Affairs) died of cardiac arrest on 6 September 2026 in Giridih, five days before this corrected pass, leaving the Urban Development & Housing portfolio vacant with no successor announced as of 11 September 2026; and Ranchi's Deputy Commissioner has changed from Manjunath Bhajantri to Varun Ranjan, IAS, per the official Ranchi district government website (ranchi.nic.in), confirming a currentness risk the original document had itself flagged (a May 2025 20-district DC reshuffle). Structurally, Chief Minister Hemant Soren personally holds Home, Personnel, Administrative Reforms, Road Construction, Building Construction, and all unallocated departments, while Transport sits with a separate cabinet minister (JMM's Deepak Birua, who also holds Revenue and Registration & Land Reforms) — meaning road engineering decisions (black-spot correction, highway design standards) run through the CM's own department rather than a separate Road Construction Minister. Congress's Radhakrishna Kishore holds Finance, Commercial Tax, Planning and Development, and Parliamentary Affairs; RJD's Sanjay Prasad Yadav holds Industries, Labour, Planning, and Training and Skill Development; Congress's Irfan Ansari holds Health, Medical Education and Family Welfare, plus Food, Public Distribution, and Consumer Affairs; and Dipika/Deepika Pandey Singh holds Rural Development/Rural Works and Panchayati Raj jointly. Jharkhand's Road Safety Lead Agency was constituted within the Department of Transport by Gazette Notification dated 26 March 2017 following a Supreme Court direction, and — because roads, transport and police sit substantially on the State List — the Government of Jharkhand's own departments, not the Union Government, are the primary point of leverage for almost all road-safety interventions CrashFree India will pursue in this state; the Union Government matters mainly for National Highway stretches, PMGSY funding rules, and the Motor Vehicles Act's national legal framework.

governance_bodies.hierarchy: The ACS/Principal Secretary/Secretary is the administrative head. The Engineer-in-Chief is the technical head, reporting directly to the administrative head. Below the E-in-C sit multiple Chief Engineers, each heading a "Wing" — at least a Central Design Organisation wing (planning, design, specification, estimation and project approval), a Communication wing (bid initiation, contracts and project execution), and a National Highway wing (all central NH projects, coordinated with MoRTH). Below Chief Engineer level the structure follows the standard PWD-style Circle → Division → Sub-Division tiering, with Divisions generally corresponding to districts.
